entries.summary: Adversaries may abuse extended attributes (xattrs) on macOS and Linux to hide their malicious data in order to evade detection. Extended attributes are key-value pairs of file and directory metadata used by both macOS and Linux.

entries.name: Stored Data Manipulation
entries.summary: Adversaries may insert, delete, or manipulate data at rest in order to influence external outcomes or hide activity, thus threatening the integrity of the data. By manipulating stored data, adversaries may attempt to affect a business process, organizational understanding, and decision making.

entries.name: Transmitted Data Manipulation
entries.summary: Adversaries may alter data en route to storage or other systems in order to manipulate external outcomes or hide activity, thus threatening the integrity of the data.

entries.name: Runtime Data Manipulation
entries.summary: Adversaries may modify systems in order to manipulate the data as it is accessed and displayed to an end user, thus threatening the integrity of the data. By manipulating runtime data, adversaries may attempt to affect a business process, organizational understanding, and decision making.

entries.name: Spearphishing Attachment
entries.summary: Adversaries may send spearphishing emails with a malicious attachment in an attempt to gain access to victim systems. Spearphishing attachment is a specific variant of spearphishing.

entries.name: Spearphishing Link
entries.summary: Adversaries may send spearphishing emails with a malicious link in an attempt to gain access to victim systems. Spearphishing with a link is a specific variant of spearphishing.

entries.name: Spearphishing via Service
entries.summary: Adversaries may send spearphishing messages via third-party services in an attempt to gain access to victim systems. Spearphishing via service is a specific variant of spearphishing.

entries.name: Spearphishing Voice
entries.summary: Adversaries may use voice communications to ultimately gain access to victim systems. Spearphishing voice is a specific variant of spearphishing.

entries.name: Exfiltration to Code Repository
entries.summary: Adversaries may exfiltrate data to a code repository rather than over their primary command and control channel. Code repositories are often accessible via an API (ex: https://api.github.com). Access to these APIs is often over HTTPS, which gives the adversary an additional level of protection.

entries.name: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
entries.summary: Adversaries may exfiltrate data to a cloud storage service rather than over their primary command and control channel. Cloud storage services allow for the storage, edit, and retrieval of data from a remote cloud storage server over the Internet.

entries.name: Exfiltration to Text Storage Sites
entries.summary: Adversaries may exfiltrate data to text storage sites instead of their primary command and control channel. Text storage sites, such as pastebin[.]com, are commonly used by developers to share code and other information.

entries.name: Exfiltration Over Webhook
entries.summary: Adversaries may exfiltrate data to a webhook endpoint rather than over their primary command and control channel. Webhooks are simple mechanisms for allowing a server to push data over HTTP/S to a client without the need for the client to continuously poll the server.

entries.name: Fast Flux DNS
entries.summary: Adversaries may use Fast Flux DNS to hide a command and control channel behind an array of rapidly changing IP addresses linked to a single domain resolution.

entries.name: Domain Generation Algorithms
entries.summary: Adversaries may make use of Domain Generation Algorithms (DGAs) to dynamically identify a destination domain for command and control traffic rather than relying on a list of static IP addresses or domains.

entries.name: DNS Calculation
entries.summary: Adversaries may perform calculations on addresses returned in DNS results to determine which port and IP address to use for command and control, rather than relying on a predetermined port number or the actual returned IP address.

entries.name: Launchctl
entries.summary: Adversaries may abuse launchctl to execute commands or programs. Launchctl interfaces with launchd, the service management framework for macOS. Launchctl supports taking subcommands on the command-line, interactively, or even redirected from standard input.

entries.name: Service Execution
entries.summary: Adversaries may abuse the Windows service control manager to execute malicious commands or payloads. The Windows service control manager (services.exe) is an interface to manage and manipulate services.

entries.name: Systemctl
entries.summary: Adversaries may abuse systemctl to execute commands or programs. Systemctl is the primary interface for systemd, the Linux init system and service manager. Typically invoked from a shell, Systemctl can also be integrated into scripts or applications.

entries.name: Symmetric Cryptography
entries.summary: Adversaries may employ a known symmetric encryption algorithm to conceal command and control traffic rather than relying on any inherent protections provided by a communication protocol. Symmetric encryption algorithms use the same key for plaintext encryption and ciphertext decryption.

entries.name: Asymmetric Cryptography
entries.summary: Adversaries may employ a known asymmetric encryption algorithm to conceal command and control traffic rather than relying on any inherent protections provided by a communication protocol.

entries.name: DLL
entries.summary: Adversaries may abuse dynamic-link library files (DLLs) in order to achieve persistence, escalate privileges, and evade defenses. DLLs are libraries that contain code and data that can be simultaneously utilized by multiple programs.

entries.name: Dylib Hijacking
entries.summary: Adversaries may execute their own payloads by placing a malicious dynamic library (dylib) with an expected name in a path a victim application searches at runtime. The dynamic loader will try to find the dylibs based on the sequential order of the search paths.

entries.name: Executable Installer File Permissions Weakness
entries.summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the binaries used by an installer. These processes may automatically execute specific binaries as part of their functionality or to perform other actions.

entries.name: Dynamic Linker Hijacking
entries.summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking environment variables the dynamic linker uses to load shared libraries.

entries.name: Path Interception by PATH Environment Variable
entries.summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking environment variables used to load libraries.

entries.name: Path Interception by Search Order Hijacking
entries.summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the search order used to load other programs.

entries.name: Path Interception by Unquoted Path
entries.summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking vulnerable file path references.

entries.name: Services File Permissions Weakness
entries.summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the binaries used by services. Adversaries may use flaws in the permissions of Windows services to replace the binary that is executed upon service start.

entries.name: Services Registry Permissions Weakness
entries.summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking the Registry entries used by services.

entries.name: COR_PROFILER
entries.summary: Adversaries may leverage the COR_PROFILER environment variable to hijack the execution flow of programs that load the .NET CLR.

entries.name: KernelCallbackTable
entries.summary: Adversaries may abuse the KernelCallbackTable of a process to hijack its execution flow in order to run their own payloads.

entries.name: AppDomainManager
entries.summary: Adversaries may execute their own malicious payloads by hijacking how the .NET `AppDomainManager` loads assemblies.

entries.name: Create Snapshot
entries.summary: An adversary may create a snapshot or data backup within a cloud account to evade defenses. A snapshot is a point-in-time copy of an existing cloud compute component such as a virtual machine (VM), virtual hard drive, or volume.

entries.name: Create Cloud Instance
entries.summary: An adversary may create a new instance or virtual machine (VM) within the compute service of a cloud account to evade defenses. Creating a new instance may allow an adversary to bypass firewall rules and permissions that exist on instances currently residing within an account.

entries.name: Delete Cloud Instance
entries.summary: An adversary may delete a cloud instance after they have performed malicious activities in an attempt to evade detection and remove evidence of their presence.

entries.name: Revert Cloud Instance
entries.summary: An adversary may revert changes made to a cloud instance after they have performed malicious activities in attempt to evade detection and remove evidence of their presence.

entries.name: Modify Cloud Compute Configurations
entries.summary: Adversaries may modify settings that directly affect the size, locations, and resources available to cloud compute infrastructure in order to evade defenses.

entries.name: Domains
entries.summary: Adversaries may acquire domains that can be used during targeting. Domain names are the human readable names used to represent one or more IP addresses. They can be purchased or, in some cases, acquired for free.

entries.name: DNS Server
entries.summary: Adversaries may set up their own Domain Name System (DNS) servers that can be used during targeting. During post-compromise activity, adversaries may utilize DNS traffic for various tasks, including for Command and Control (ex: Application Layer Protocol).

entries.name: Virtual Private Server
entries.summary: Adversaries may rent Virtual Private Servers (VPSs) that can be used during targeting. There exist a variety of cloud service providers that will sell virtual machines/containers as a service. By utilizing a VPS, adversaries can make it difficult to physically tie back operations to them.

entries.name: Server
entries.summary: Adversaries may buy, lease, rent, or obtain physical servers that can be used during targeting. Use of servers allows an adversary to stage, launch, and execute an operation.

entries.name: Botnet
entries.summary: Adversaries may buy, lease, or rent a network of compromised systems that can be used during targeting. A botnet is a network of compromised systems that can be instructed to perform coordinated tasks.

entries.name: Web Services
entries.summary: Adversaries may register for web services that can be used during targeting. A variety of popular websites exist for adversaries to register for a web-based service that can be abused during later stages of the adversary lifecycle, such as during Command and Control (Web Service), Exfiltration…

entries.name: Serverless
entries.summary: Adversaries may purchase and configure serverless cloud infrastructure, such as Cloudflare Workers, AWS Lambda functions, or Google Apps Scripts, that can be used during targeting.

entries.name: Malvertising
entries.summary: Adversaries may purchase online advertisements that can be abused to distribute malware to victims. Ads can be purchased to plant as well as favorably position artifacts in specific locations online, such as prominently placed within search engine results.

entries.name: Domains
entries.summary: Adversaries may hijack domains and/or subdomains that can be used during targeting. Domain registration hijacking is the act of changing the registration of a domain name without the permission of the original registrant.

entries.name: DNS Server
entries.summary: Adversaries may compromise third-party DNS servers that can be used during targeting. During post-compromise activity, adversaries may utilize DNS traffic for various tasks, including for Command and Control (ex: Application Layer Protocol).

entries.name: Virtual Private Server
entries.summary: Adversaries may compromise third-party Virtual Private Servers (VPSs) that can be used during targeting. There exist a variety of cloud service providers that will sell virtual machines/containers as a service. Adversaries may compromise VPSs purchased by third-party entities.

entries.name: Server
entries.summary: Adversaries may compromise third-party servers that can be used during targeting. Use of servers allows an adversary to stage, launch, and execute an operation. During post-compromise activity, adversaries may utilize servers for various tasks, including for Command and Control.

entries.name: Botnet
entries.summary: Adversaries may compromise numerous third-party systems to form a botnet that can be used during targeting. A botnet is a network of compromised systems that can be instructed to perform coordinated tasks.

entries.name: Web Services
entries.summary: Adversaries may compromise access to third-party web services that can be used during targeting. A variety of popular websites exist for legitimate users to register for web-based services, such as GitHub, Twitter, Dropbox, Google, SendGrid, etc.

entries.name: Serverless
entries.summary: Adversaries may compromise serverless cloud infrastructure, such as Cloudflare Workers, AWS Lambda functions, or Google Apps Scripts, that can be used during targeting.

entries.name: Network Devices
entries.summary: Adversaries may compromise third-party network devices that can be used during targeting.

entries.name: Social Media Accounts
entries.summary: Adversaries may create and cultivate social media accounts that can be used during targeting. Adversaries can create social media accounts that can be used to build a persona to further operations.

entries.name: Email Accounts
entries.summary: Adversaries may create email accounts that can be used during targeting. Adversaries can use accounts created with email providers to further their operations, such as leveraging them to conduct Phishing for Information or Phishing.

entries.name: Cloud Accounts
entries.summary: Adversaries may create accounts with cloud providers that can be used during targeting.

entries.name: Social Media Accounts
entries.summary: Adversaries may compromise social media accounts that can be used during targeting. For operations incorporating social engineering, the utilization of an online persona may be important. Rather than creating and cultivating social media profiles (i.e.

entries.name: Email Accounts
entries.summary: Adversaries may compromise email accounts that can be used during targeting. Adversaries can use compromised email accounts to further their operations, such as leveraging them to conduct Phishing for Information, Phishing, or large-scale spam email campaigns.

entries.name: Cloud Accounts
entries.summary: Adversaries may compromise cloud accounts that can be used during targeting. Adversaries can use compromised cloud accounts to further their operations, including leveraging cloud storage services such as Dropbox, Microsoft OneDrive, or AWS S3 buckets for Exfiltration to Cloud Storage or to Upload…

entries.name: Malware
entries.summary: Adversaries may develop malware and malware components that can be used during targeting.

entries.name: Code Signing Certificates
entries.summary: Adversaries may create self-signed code signing certificates that can be used during targeting. Code signing is the process of digitally signing executables and scripts to confirm the software author and guarantee that the code has not been altered or corrupted.

entries.name: Digital Certificates
entries.summary: Adversaries may create self-signed SSL/TLS certificates that can be used during targeting. SSL/TLS certificates are designed to instill trust.

entries.name: Exploits
entries.summary: Adversaries may develop exploits that can be used during targeting. An exploit takes advantage of a bug or vulnerability in order to cause unintended or unanticipated behavior to occur on computer hardware or software.

entries.name: Malware
entries.summary: Adversaries may buy, steal, or download malware that can be used during targeting. Malicious software can include payloads, droppers, post-compromise tools, backdoors, packers, and C2 protocols.

entries.name: Tool
entries.summary: Adversaries may buy, steal, or download software tools that can be used during targeting. Tools can be open or closed source, free or commercial. A tool can be used for malicious purposes by an adversary, but (unlike malware) were not intended to be used for those purposes (ex: PsExec).

entries.name: Code Signing Certificates
entries.summary: Adversaries may buy and/or steal code signing certificates that can be used during targeting. Code signing is the process of digitally signing executables and scripts to confirm the software author and guarantee that the code has not been altered or corrupted.

entries.name: Digital Certificates
entries.summary: Adversaries may buy and/or steal SSL/TLS certificates that can be used during targeting. SSL/TLS certificates are designed to instill trust.

entries.name: Exploits
entries.summary: Adversaries may buy, steal, or download exploits that can be used during targeting. An exploit takes advantage of a bug or vulnerability in order to cause unintended or unanticipated behavior to occur on computer hardware or software.

entries.name: Vulnerabilities
entries.summary: Adversaries may acquire information about vulnerabilities that can be used during targeting. A vulnerability is a weakness in computer hardware or software that can, potentially, be exploited by an adversary to cause unintended or unanticipated behavior to occur.

entries.name: Artificial Intelligence
entries.summary: Adversaries may obtain access to generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools, such as large language models (LLMs), to aid various techniques during targeting.

entries.name: Credentials
entries.summary: Adversaries may gather credentials that can be used during targeting. Account credentials gathered by adversaries may be those directly associated with the target victim organization or attempt to take advantage of the tendency for users to use the same passwords across personal and business…

entries.name: Email Addresses
entries.summary: Adversaries may gather email addresses that can be used during targeting. Even if internal instances exist, organizations may have public-facing email infrastructure and addresses for employees.

entries.name: Employee Names
entries.summary: Adversaries may gather employee names that can be used during targeting. Employee names can be used to derive email addresses as well as to help guide other reconnaissance efforts and/or craft more-believable lures.

entries.name: Domain Properties
entries.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's network domain(s) that can be used during targeting.

entries.name: DNS
entries.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's DNS that can be used during targeting. DNS information may include a variety of details, including registered name servers as well as records that outline addressing for a target’s subdomains, mail servers, and other hosts.

entries.name: Network Trust Dependencies
entries.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's network trust dependencies that can be used during targeting.

entries.name: Network Topology
entries.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's network topology that can be used during targeting. Information about network topologies may include a variety of details, including the physical and/or logical arrangement of both external-facing and internal network environments.

entries.name: IP Addresses
entries.summary: Adversaries may gather the victim's IP addresses that can be used during targeting. Public IP addresses may be allocated to organizations by block, or a range of sequential addresses. Information about assigned IP addresses may include a variety of details, such as which IP addresses are in use.

entries.name: Network Security Appliances
entries.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's network security appliances that can be used during targeting. Information about network security appliances may include a variety of details, such as the existence and specifics of deployed firewalls, content filters, and proxies/bastion hosts.

entries.name: Determine Physical Locations
entries.summary: Adversaries may gather the victim's physical location(s) that can be used during targeting. Information about physical locations of a target organization may include a variety of details, including where key resources and infrastructure are housed.

entries.name: Business Relationships
entries.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's business relationships that can be used during targeting.

entries.name: Identify Business Tempo
entries.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's business tempo that can be used during targeting. Information about an organization’s business tempo may include a variety of details, including operational hours/days of the week.

entries.name: Identify Roles
entries.summary: Adversaries may gather information about identities and roles within the victim organization that can be used during targeting.

entries.name: Hardware
entries.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's host hardware that can be used during targeting.

entries.name: Software
entries.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's host software that can be used during targeting.

entries.name: Firmware
entries.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's host firmware that can be used during targeting.

entries.name: Client Configurations
entries.summary: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's client configurations that can be used during targeting.

entries.name: Social Media
entries.summary: Adversaries may search social media for information about victims that can be used during targeting. Social media sites may contain various information about a victim organization, such as business announcements as well as information about the roles, locations, and interests of staff.

entries.name: Search Engines
entries.summary: Adversaries may use search engines to collect information about victims that can be used during targeting. Search engine services typically crawl online sites to index content and may provide users with specialized syntax to search for specific keywords or specific types of content (i.e.

entries.name: Code Repositories
entries.summary: Adversaries may search public code repositories for information about victims that can be used during targeting. Victims may store code in repositories on various third-party websites such as GitHub, GitLab, SourceForge, and BitBucket.

entries.name: Scanning IP Blocks
entries.summary: Adversaries may scan victim IP blocks to gather information that can be used during targeting. Public IP addresses may be allocated to organizations by block, or a range of sequential addresses.

entries.name: Vulnerability Scanning
entries.summary: Adversaries may scan victims for vulnerabilities that can be used during targeting. Vulnerability scans typically check if the configuration of a target host/application (ex: software and version) potentially aligns with the target of a specific exploit the adversary may seek to use.

entries.name: Wordlist Scanning
entries.summary: Adversaries may iteratively probe infrastructure using brute-forcing and crawling techniques. While this technique employs similar methods to Brute Force, its goal is the identification of content and infrastructure rather than the discovery of valid credentials.

entries.name: DNS/Passive DNS
entries.summary: Adversaries may search DNS data for information about victims that can be used during targeting. DNS information may include a variety of details, including registered name servers as well as records that outline addressing for a target’s subdomains, mail servers, and other hosts.

entries.name: WHOIS
entries.summary: Adversaries may search public WHOIS data for information about victims that can be used during targeting. WHOIS data is stored by regional Internet registries (RIR) responsible for allocating and assigning Internet resources such as domain names.

entries.name: Digital Certificates
entries.summary: Adversaries may search public digital certificate data for information about victims that can be used during targeting. Digital certificates are issued by a certificate authority (CA) in order to cryptographically verify the origin of signed content.

entries.name: CDNs
entries.summary: Adversaries may search content delivery network (CDN) data about victims that can be used during targeting. CDNs allow an organization to host content from a distributed, load balanced array of servers.

entries.name: Scan Databases
entries.summary: Adversaries may search within public scan databases for information about victims that can be used during targeting.

entries.name: Threat Intel Vendors
entries.summary: Adversaries may search private data from threat intelligence vendors for information that can be used during targeting. Threat intelligence vendors may offer paid feeds or portals that offer more data than what is publicly reported.

entries.name: Purchase Technical Data
entries.summary: Adversaries may purchase technical information about victims that can be used during targeting. Information about victims may be available for purchase within reputable private sources and databases, such as paid subscriptions to feeds of scan databases or other data aggregation services.

entries.name: Spearphishing Service
entries.summary: Adversaries may send spearphishing messages via third-party services to elicit sensitive information that can be used during targeting. Spearphishing for information is an attempt to trick targets into divulging information, frequently credentials or other actionable information.

entries.name: Spearphishing Attachment
entries.summary: Adversaries may send spearphishing messages with a malicious attachment to elicit sensitive information that can be used during targeting. Spearphishing for information is an attempt to trick targets into divulging information, frequently credentials or other actionable information.

entries.name: Spearphishing Link
entries.summary: Adversaries may send spearphishing messages with a malicious link to elicit sensitive information that can be used during targeting. Spearphishing for information is an attempt to trick targets into divulging information, frequently credentials or other actionable information.

entries.name: Spearphishing Voice
entries.summary: Adversaries may use voice communications to elicit sensitive information that can be used during targeting. Spearphishing for information is an attempt to trick targets into divulging information, frequently credentials or other actionable information.

entries.name: Network Address Translation Traversal
entries.summary: Adversaries may bridge network boundaries by modifying a network device’s Network Address Translation (NAT) configuration. Malicious modifications to NAT may enable an adversary to bypass restrictions on traffic routing that otherwise separate trusted and untrusted networks.

entries.name: Reduce Key Space
entries.summary: Adversaries may reduce the level of effort required to decrypt data transmitted over the network by reducing the cipher strength of encrypted communications.

entries.name: Disable Crypto Hardware
entries.summary: Adversaries disable a network device’s dedicated hardware encryption, which may enable them to leverage weaknesses in software encryption in order to reduce the effort involved in collecting, manipulating, and exfiltrating transmitted data.

entries.name: Patch System Image
entries.summary: Adversaries may modify the operating system of a network device to introduce new capabilities or weaken existing defenses. Some network devices are built with a monolithic architecture, where the entire operating system and most of the functionality of the device is contained within a single file.

entries.name: Downgrade System Image
entries.summary: Adversaries may install an older version of the operating system of a network device to weaken security. Older operating system versions on network devices often have weaker encryption ciphers and, in general, fewer/less updated defensive features.

entries.name: SNMP (MIB Dump)
entries.summary: Adversaries may target the Management Information Base (MIB) to collect and/or mine valuable information in a network managed using Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP).

entries.name: Network Device Configuration Dump
entries.summary: Adversaries may access network configuration files to collect sensitive data about the device and the network. The network configuration is a file containing parameters that determine the operation of the device.

entries.name: Web Cookies
entries.summary: Adversaries may forge web cookies that can be used to gain access to web applications or Internet services. Web applications and services (hosted in cloud SaaS environments or on-premise servers) often use session cookies to authenticate and authorize user access.

entries.name: SAML Tokens
entries.summary: An adversary may forge SAML tokens with any permissions claims and lifetimes if they possess a valid SAML token-signing certificate.

entries.name: Upload Malware
entries.summary: Adversaries may upload malware to third-party or adversary controlled infrastructure to make it accessible during targeting. Malicious software can include payloads, droppers, post-compromise tools, backdoors, and a variety of other malicious content.

entries.name: Upload Tool
entries.summary: Adversaries may upload tools to third-party or adversary controlled infrastructure to make it accessible during targeting. Tools can be open or closed source, free or commercial.

entries.name: Install Digital Certificate
entries.summary: Adversaries may install SSL/TLS certificates that can be used during targeting. SSL/TLS certificates are files that can be installed on servers to enable secure communications between systems.

entries.name: Drive-by Target
entries.summary: Adversaries may prepare an operational environment to infect systems that visit a website over the normal course of browsing. Endpoint systems may be compromised through browsing to adversary controlled sites, as in Drive-by Compromise.

entries.name: Link Target
entries.summary: Adversaries may put in place resources that are referenced by a link that can be used during targeting. An adversary may rely upon a user clicking a malicious link in order to divulge information (including credentials) or to gain execution, as in Malicious Link.

entries.name: SEO Poisoning
entries.summary: Adversaries may poison mechanisms that influence search engine optimization (SEO) to further lure staged capabilities towards potential victims.

entries.name: AI Result Poisoning
entries.summary: Adversaries may manipulate publicly accessible web content to influence generative AI systems or AI-powered search engines into retrieving, citing, or recommending attacker-controlled information.

entries.name: System Language Discovery
entries.summary: Adversaries may attempt to gather information about the system language of a victim in order to infer the geographical location of that host. This information may be used to shape follow-on behaviors, including whether the adversary infects the target and/or attempts specific actions.

entries.name: Written Content
entries.summary: Adversaries may create or tailor written materials to support targeting and malicious operations.

entries.name: Audio-Visual Content
entries.summary: Adversaries may create or manipulate audio, image, and video content to support targeting and malicious operations.

entries.name: Impersonation
entries.summary: Adversaries may impersonate a trusted person or organization in order to persuade and trick a target into performing some action on their behalf.

entries.name: Email Spoofing
entries.summary: Adversaries may fake, or spoof, a sender’s identity by modifying the value of relevant email headers in order to establish contact with victims under false pretenses. In addition to actual email content, email headers (such as the FROM header, which contains the email address of the sender) may…

entries.name: Disable or Modify Windows Event Log
entries.summary: Adversaries may disable or modify the Windows Event Log to limit data that can be leveraged for detections and audits. Windows Event Log records user and system activity such as login attempts and process creation. This data is used by security tools and analysts to generate detections.

entries.name: Disable or Modify Cloud Log
entries.summary: An adversary may disable or modify cloud logging capabilities and integrations to limit what data is collected on their activities and avoid detection.

entries.name: Modify or Spoof Tool UI
entries.summary: Adversaries may spoof or manipulate security tool user interfaces (UIs) to falsely indicate tools are functioning normally and delay detection and response.

entries.name: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System Log
entries.summary: Adversaries may disable or modify the Linux Audit system to hide malicious activity and avoid detection. Linux admins use the Linux Audit system to track security-relevant information on a system.

entries.name: Clear Windows Event Logs
entries.summary: Adversaries may clear Windows Event Logs to hide the activity of an intrusion. Windows Event Logs are a record of a computer's alerts and notifications.

entries.name: Clear Linux or Mac System Logs
entries.summary: Adversaries may clear system logs to hide evidence of an intrusion. macOS and Linux both keep track of system or user-initiated actions via system logs. The majority of native system logging is stored under the `/var/log/` directory.

entries.name: Impair Autonomous Defenses
entries.summary: Adversaries may use methods like Indirect Prompt Injection to disrupt, disable, or otherwise impair autonomous defensive capabilities such as LLM-assisted processing of malware, artifacts, or activity.

entries.name: Cloud Firewall
entries.summary: Adversaries may disable or modify a firewall within a cloud environment to bypass controls that limit access to cloud resources.

entries.name: Network Device Firewall
entries.summary: Adversaries may disable network device-based firewall mechanisms entirely or add, delete, or modify particular rules in order to bypass controls limiting network usage.

entries.name: Windows Host Firewall
entries.summary: Adversaries may disable or modify the Windows host firewall to bypass controls limiting network usage.

entries.name: Automate CAPTCHA Completion
entries.summary: Adversaries may attempt to use bots to successfully solve CAPTCHA challenges. CAPTCHA challenges are typically used by defenders to detect and prevent bot and spam traffic from accessing protected webpages. CAPTCHAs are automated tests often placed before login screens or form fields.

entries.name: Avoid CAPTCHA
entries.summary: Adversaries may avoid CAPTCHA challenges by mimicking human behavior. Automation tests, such as CAPTCHA, are typically used by defenders to detect and prevent bot and spam traffic from accessing protected webpages. CAPTCHAs are often placed before login screens or form fields.
